narrationScript: Pointers are incredibly versatile, especially when working with arrays. In C, an array's name often behaves like a pointer to its first element. For instance, if you have `int arr[5];`, then `arr` itself can be treated as `&arr[0]`. This allows for pointer arithmetic. If `ptr` points to `arr[0]`, then `ptr + 1` will point to `arr[1]`. This is because pointer arithmetic automatically scales by the size of the data type it points to. So, if integers are 4 bytes, `ptr + 1` actually adds 4 bytes to the address. You can iterate through an array using a pointer, which can sometimes be more efficient than using an index. However, be careful not to go out of bounds. For example, `ptr + 5` for an `arr[5]` would point to memory outside the array, potentially corrupting data or causing a crash. Always ensure your pointer arithmetic stays within the bounds of allocated memory.
